nameStory: This tiny sea snail is named after Green, likely a 19th-century naturalist or collector who helped scientists discover this species. The scientific name Cerithiopsis comes from Greek, meaning 'resembling a Cerithium' - another type of spiral-shelled marine snail that this little guy looks like, only much smaller.
description: Green's cerithiopsis is a minuscule sea snail that you'd need a magnifying glass to properly appreciate. These marine gastropods have tall, slender spiral shells that twist upward like tiny spires, rarely growing larger than a few millimeters. They belong to a family of very small sea snails that live on the ocean floor, creeping along surfaces in search of microscopic food. Despite their tiny size, they're true mollusks with all the same body parts as their giant conch cousins - just shrunk down to nearly invisible proportions.

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Tall, narrow spiral shell that tapers to a sharp point, like a miniature church steeple - much taller than it is wide

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small - typically just a few millimeters long, easily mistaken for a grain of sand or tiny shell fragment

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: Smooth to slightly ribbed surface with a glossy appearance when wet, feeling almost glassy if you can handle one carefully

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Usually pale brown, tan, or whitish - often translucent enough to see through when held up to light

idTips.label: Spiral pattern
idTips.description: Multiple whorls (spiral sections) that are clearly visible even at small size, creating distinct ridged lines around the shell

habitat: Look for Green's cerithiopsis in deeper waters of the Gulf of Maine, typically on sandy or muddy bottoms where they crawl among debris and sediment. They're most often found by beachcombers in shell drift - the accumulations of small shells and marine debris that wash up after storms. You're more likely to encounter their empty shells than live specimens, as they live in subtidal zones beyond the reach of typical tide pooling.

seasonality.spring: Empty shells may begin washing ashore with spring storms, mixed in with other small shell debris along the tide line.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for finding shells in drift material, as calmer weather allows more thorough beach exploration and better visibility of tiny specimens.
seasonality.fall: Storm activity increases shell deposition on beaches. Fall storms often bring up material from deeper waters where these snails live.
seasonality.winter: Harsh winter storms can deposit shells, but cold weather makes beach searching less pleasant and shells may be buried quickly by shifting sand.

funFact: These snails are so small that an entire living population could fit comfortably in a teaspoon, yet they're active predators that hunt even tinier organisms - making them some of the ocean's most miniaturized hunters!
confusionNotes: Green's cerithiopsis can be confused with juvenile shells of larger spiral snails, but remember the size rule: if it's bigger than a few millimeters, it's probably something else entirely. Other tiny marine snails might have similar spiral shells, but most are either more rounded or have different proportions - Green's maintains that distinctive tall, slender 'church spire' shape.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of sightings in New England (only one recorded observation) means this species is either very uncommon in our waters, extremely difficult to spot due to its tiny size, or both. Most encounters with this species will be finding empty shells rather than live animals, as they live in deeper waters offshore.
compareHints: Since Green's cerithiopsis appears to be the only member of its genus documented in New England waters, compare it to other tiny marine snails in the region. Unlike the more common periwinkles which have rounded, squat shells, or slipper shells which are flattened, Green's cerithiopsis maintains that distinctively tall, narrow spiral form that sets it apart from most other small marine gastropods you'll encounter.
